Tools of light —
fixtures, beams, and light in software

Learning lighting is not memorizing fixture names; it is knowing which tool controls the size · distance · angle · intensity · color of light. This feature puts on one map the real fixtures and modifiers used on set, the beams from pin spot to ambient, and the After Effects · Premiere functions that rebuild the same light.

<small>SPREAD 05</small>Light in software — four After Effects 3D lights and light-effect tools

After Effects 3D lights are a scale model of set lighting. They use the same vocabulary (spot · point · ambient) and control the same properties (intensity · color · cone angle · falloff · shadow). If you can handle light on set, you will make the same calls in software.

feature_ppm.html:
PPM,
the last agreement before the shoot

PPM stands for pre-production meeting. It is both the meeting just before shooting, where client · planning · direction · production lock every decision, and the document that records it. The approved PPM document becomes the reference for any later dispute. A verbal agreement that is not recorded does not exist. This feature walks through one PPM deck, page by page.
The same change can cost up to 50x more, depending on when you make it
Fixes on paper — the only cost is time
← the last flat stretch before the cost curve bends

<small>SPREAD 01 · Directing intent</small>Tone and manner board — the page that turns adjectives into measurements

"Warm and sophisticated" is not an agreement. A tone and manner board translates adjectives into measurable values of color temperature · contrast · saturation · texture · pace, so that camera · art · post look at the same numbers. Always review references together on screen. Describe a tone in words, and everyone imagines it differently.

Plate PPM-1 Tone and manner board — three adjectives, five references and one anti-reference, a palette. One sheet becomes the common language of camera · art · post.
Apply the palette equally to wardrobe · props · background · graphics. Send the swatch codes to the art and post teams in the same file.

In each reference panel, always write one word for "what you are referencing" (light · color · texture · movement · people). Copy a whole reference and it is plagiarism; take one element and it is study. The single anti-reference panel saves more meeting time than any other.

feature_storyboard.html:
The storyboard,
a promise made in pictures

A storyboard is a matter of information design, not drawing skill. This feature sets out in one place what a panel must say for ten people to shoot the same scene, and how the panel changes across media: horizontal · vertical · ultra-wide · 360 · curved · facade · AR/VR/MR/XR.
G-18 Storyboarding — write shot · movement · time in every panel. The drawing can be rough; the information cannot.
01ContinuityThe director sorting out ideas. Rough drawings, several versions compared, for internal meetings. 1–2 hours.
02StoryboardThe blueprint for the whole crew. Exact framing · timing · sound. Minimal changes after PPM approval. 1–2 days.
03AnimaticThe boards on a timeline with temp music · narration. Rhythm and length problems show at once. 2–3 days.
For a 15-second ad or a 1-minute short-form piece, go all the way to an animatic. Rhythm problems do not show in still pictures.

The storyboard is the last point in the production pipeline where mistakes are cheap to fix. If a change at the concept stage costs 1, it costs 3 at the board stage, 20 on shoot day, and 50 in post. So a board is not a document for drawing nicely but a document for getting it wrong fast.

<small>SPREAD 04</small>360 · VR boards — design an 'axis of attention,' not a timeline

Media facade — elevation pixel map + viewing distanceMinimum viewing distance (m) ≈ pixel pitch (mm) · text height is 1/250 of distance → effectively no text, only shape and color · simulate at three points: walking 20 m / across the street 60 m / far view 150 m

<small>SPREAD 06</small>AR · MR · XR boards — the panel splits into 'layers'

An AR · MR panel is not one flat drawing; it breaks down into reality layer / tracked surface / virtual object layer / UI layer. And "what the audience must do to reach the next panel (interaction)" replaces the transition mark. An XR stage (LED-wall virtual production) works the other way: the board splits into four tracks of camera · LED background · physical set · lighting.

AR — the panel splits into layersDraw four layers separately: reality / tracked surface / virtual object / UI · instead of transition marks, "what must happen to reach the next panel" (tap · rotate · approach) · one failure-branch panel is a must

MR — draw on a map of the roomVirtual objects attach to wall · floor · table anchors · real furniture must occlude virtual objects for them to be believed · movement radius 2 m; never lead users outside the guardian
XR stage — a four-track boardPhysical set · actors / LED background (Unreal) / camera tracking / lighting sync as four lines per cut · note inner/outer frustum, plate version, wall brightness

Preface — why this book, why now

The video production environment of 2026 is richer than a decade ago by any measure. The device in your pocket shoots 4K, free editing software yields commercial results, and a few sentences conjure scenes that never existed. What the learner needs now is neither equipment nor information. It is order.

That is exactly where the problem begins. When information is scattered without limit, learners cannot tell what to learn first. They pick up color grading before aperture, and download transition effects before understanding the cut. More tools, fewer finished works — the paradox comes from here. Search gives you knowledge, but not the arrangement of knowledge.

Generative AI has widened the gap. The bar for output has dropped; the bar for judgment has risen. The old proposition that stronger tools raise the value of people who know the principles has never been confirmed so plainly.

This book is an attempt to provide that arrangement. From what video is, through language, technique and planning, to media, market and career, it lays one path a person can walk from beginning to end. Each part stands alone so you can start in the middle, and read in order they form a single narrative.

At the same time, this book is intensely practical. The chapter after explaining why shutter speed is fixed gives setting presets by camera model; the chapter after explaining what a storyboard means gives the full notation set and blank templates. Learn principle and execution apart and each is half of itself. The tables and checklists here are not for reading but for opening on set.

Finally, employment gets a part of its own. Most people who pick up this book want to make a living from video. Knowing which companies hire whom, what a portfolio must prove, and how to survive the first three months is a skill too. A textbook that does not teach it is only half honest.
Author's note — on making a model for teaching

Video production grew up as an industry before it was established as a discipline. The field has accumulated a vast body of practice, but texts that organize it into a system are rare. Shooting lives in camera manuals, editing in software guides, careers in job-hunting material, and the learner must stitch the pieces together alone. That stitching is hardest for the beginner, because knowing what to learn first already demands considerable knowledge.

The teaching side is no different. In a field without a standard textbook, lectures depend on personal experience. Experience is vivid but not reproducible. Reproducibility is the minimum requirement of education, and it begins with a shared text.

This book is an attempt to make that text once. The goal is not a finished canon but a floor on which later revisions and rebuttals can stand. So the content was selected by one criterion: will it still hold in five years? Menu locations in particular software and specs of particular cameras appear only minimally; the pages go to the order of judgment instead. Tools get replaced; the order does not.

The structure assumes both the first-time learner and the person teaching them. Each part opens with a narrative introduction to set context, arranges the knowledge item by item, and closes with a one-page summary ready for class use. All plates are monochrome — a practical decision so that nothing is lost in black-and-white copies or on low-resolution projectors.

The same reason governs the part on generative AI, which centers on where in the pipeline to place what, rather than how to operate individual services. Tools live short lives; structures live long ones. In an environment where anyone can make a plausible picture, education's share is not the transfer of functions but the training of judgment.

A word on the handling of examples. This book reproduces no frame from any existing work. All diagrams were designed from scratch; figure and equipment drawings and reference images were made with generative image models, with the generation conditions disclosed in the appendix. A text that teaches how to make good video should not be built on other people's results.

If this book becomes someone's first textbook, someone's syllabus, or lies open on someone's desk on set, it has done its job. Tell me where the explanation stalls and where it did not fit the field; that is where the next edition begins.
Spring 2026, Jia Ahn

Q01Should I buy a camera first, or lights?
Lights. On the same budget, an entry camera with lighting beats a high-end camera without it. (PART 4)
Q02Can I make commercial video on a smartphone?
Yes, provided you turn off auto exposure and auto white balance and use an external mic. (3.13)
Q0324fps or 30fps?
24 for emotional ads and brand films; 30 is the safe choice for informational and caption-heavy videos. (3.8)
Q04Do I really need 4K?
Shoot 4K even if the final is FHD. It leaves room for reframing and vertical crops. (3.7)
Q05Is log always better?
Only when you will grade in post. For chroma key shoots it is actually a disadvantage. (3.10)
Q06Which editing program should I learn first?
By domestic hiring standards, the Premiere Pro and After Effects combination. (5.3)
Q07Can I cut in After Effects?
Not recommended. A tool that handles time horizontally and a tool that handles layers vertically have different jobs. (5.5)
Q08My composites keep looking pasted on
Check three things: black level, atmospheric perspective, grain. (5.7)
Q09How far should color grading go?
Match exposure and white balance, match shot to shot, then apply the look. The order matters. (5.8)
Q10Where do I get music?
Subscription license libraries are safest. Keep the purchase record in the project folder. (4.9)
Q11Is a short clip fine, copyright-wise?
No such rule exists. It is infringement regardless of length. (7.7)
Q12I can't draw storyboards. What do I do?
Drawing skill is not required. Boxes and arrows suffice; the notation rules matter more. (2.1)
Q13What do I do when planning stalls?
Write down 20 pain points of the target and pick the ones the product solves. The safest method. (2.5)
Q14Can't I fit two messages into 15 seconds?
Both vanish. Keep one. (7.1)
Q15How do I build the first 3 seconds?
Pick one of the six types, and never open with a logo and a fade. (7.2)
Q16I'm not getting views
Check reach, click-through, retention and engagement, in that order, and the cause narrows. (8.8)
Q17How long should a title be?
40–60 characters, with the key words in the first 25. (8.11)
Q18How many hashtags?
Mix large, medium and small ones, around 10–15. (8.4)
Q19Can I just crop horizontal footage for vertical?
Shoot 4K and mark vertical guides at the shooting stage. The composition itself changes. (6.2)
Q20Where do short-form captions go?
Center, about one third up from the bottom. The top 12% and bottom 20% are covered by UI. (6.3)
Q21Can I make a whole video with AI?
Replace the entire process and consistency collapses. Limit it to three points: ideation, drafts, automation. (8.9)
Q22Do I have to disclose AI use?
Disclosure requirements are growing in competitions and client deliveries. Record your usage in the documents. (8.9)
Q23How many pieces in a portfolio?
5–8. Your weakest piece is read as your level. (10.3)
Q24I have no experience. What do I put in?
Finished personal work and its process material. Commissioned work is not the only kind that counts. (10.3)
Q25How long should a showreel be?
60–90 seconds. Past 2 minutes nobody watches to the end. (10.4)
Q26What gets asked most in interviews?
"Walk us through one portfolio piece." Answer in order: intent, problem, solution, result. (10.6)
Q27Where is a good first job?
An organization small enough to observe the whole process. Your first role is not your final identity. (10.1)
Q28When should I go freelance?
After you have three months of living costs saved and can write a quote and a contract. (10.10)
Q29The revision requests never end
Because the contract did not state the number of revisions. Usually limit it to 2–3. (9.5)
Q30I feel like I've plateaued
Work on your sound. It is the fastest improvement when you've been staring only at the picture. (4.10)

PART 01
Introduction

The first wall anyone who sets out to learn video hits is not technique but information overload. There are tens of thousands of videos on camera settings, editing programs change their interface every year, and since 2022 generative AI has joined in, so what you learned yesterday is outdated today. Many people wear out chasing tools.

Step back a little and the picture changes. When the Lumière brothers filmed a train arriving in 1895, the questions were already there: how much to put in the frame, how long to show it. The principles the Soviet filmmakers discovered experimenting with montage in the 1920s still drive the cut editing of short-form today. Tools change every 10 years; the language of video has stood almost still for over 100.

That is why this part starts with history. Know why 24 frames, why a 180-degree shutter, why faces grow as screens shrink, and your judgment holds when a new tool appears. This is not about memorizing a timeline. It is about understanding what constraints and compromises produced each standard we now take for granted.
Background 1
What does the moving image hold on to?

Video is a technique for recording light and an old desire to hold on to time. In "The Ontology of the Photographic Image" (1945), the French critic André Bazin traced the origin of the plastic arts to the Egyptian mummy: the desire to preserve the body's form against death, the "mummy complex." Photography is special because light, not a human hand, leaves the trace of the object directly, and cinema goes a step further and embalms time itself.

Around the same time, Walter Benjamin asked an entirely different question in "The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction" (first draft 1935). A painting has a uniqueness that exists only here and now, its "aura." But photography and film reproduce the same image endlessly, and audiences meet it in theaters and living rooms. Benjamin saw this change as toppling the authority of art while opening a new mode of perception to the masses. A short video reaching millions of phones at once sits at the far edge of the world he foresaw.

So how do still photographs appear to move? For a long time textbooks explained it with "persistence of vision": the image lingering on the retina overlaps the next one. But since Max Wertheimer's apparent-motion experiments of 1912, researchers understand motion perception as the brain's interpretation rather than the retina's. Two lights flashing alternately at the right interval feel like one light moving. Video is ultimately an illusion completed inside the viewer's brain, and that fact is the starting point for understanding editing and animation.

In the two volumes of Cinema in the 1980s, the philosopher Gilles Deleuze divided the film image into the "movement-image" and the "time-image." In classical cinema time flows along a chain of action and reaction. In postwar European cinema, scenes where characters cannot act and merely look, and time that drifts without purpose, began to fill the screen. An ad that tries to provoke a response within 3 seconds speaks the language of the movement-image; a brand film that leaves room with long takes borrows the sense of the time-image.

Every technique in this book returns to three questions. What to hold on to, whom to deliver it to, and what to let complete itself in the viewer's mind. The video maker is a technician of light and a designer of the audience's perception and memory.

Further reading — André Bazin, "The Ontology of the Photographic Image," What Is Cinema? · Walter Benjamin, "The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction" · Gilles Deleuze, Cinema 1: The Movement-Image, Cinema 2: The Time-Image

PART 01What is video?
Working principles from history
Six working principles drawn from history. What 130 years of history left behind is not a timeline but six sentences you can put straight into a proposal today.
P01-PRINCIPLES A classroom learning principles from historyA professor pointing to a film still projected on the wall, students with notebooks open
Note Rather than memorizing a timeline, this section aims to draw from a single scene a principle you can use now

01The medium makes the form. Screen size, viewing distance, ambient noise and controls decide a piece's length and shot sizes. Start planning without choosing a platform and you will end up remaking it.
02Meaning lies between cuts. A principle unchanged since Kuleshov. Before gathering good material, decide the order you will join it in.
03New technology is a constraint first. A new tool narrows expression at first. Use it before others do, but put it in the final piece only when you can absorb its limits into your direction.
04Standards are conventions. 24fps, 16:9 and the 180-degree shutter are agreements, not laws of physics. Know the reasons and you can break them on purpose.
05Smaller screen, bigger everything. As the screen shrinks, subjects get bigger, cuts get shorter and captions grow. The core rule for mobile.

06Distribution changes creation. Since YouTube removed the distribution barrier, planning starts not from the idea but from discoverability. That is why titles and thumbnails became part of directing.
TIP
Don't explain the principle in words; show it on screen.

PART 01What is video?
The birth and principles of photography
A story from the dark room to the smartphone. Photography was born before video, and nearly every video technology stands on photographic technology.
A camera is a hole that gathers light and a surface that receives it
① Pinhole — light travels straightThe outside scene passes through a tiny hole and lands upside down on the wall. The smaller the hole, the sharper and darker
② Lens — gathers light to a pointGlass bends light so the image is both bright and sharp. The aperture sets the amount, the shutter the time
③ Recording surface — from silver to electricityIn film, exposed silver grains turn black; in a sensor, pixels turn light into charge
Figure 3 How a camera works — starting from a single pinhole, it was completed as lens · aperture · shutter · recording surface were added in turn.
Term
Camera obscura — Latin for 'dark room'. Light entering through a small hole projects the outside scene upside down on the opposite wall.
Photography began with attempts to fix with chemicals this image, which painters had used since the Renaissance as a drawing aid.
The five elements of a camera
01Dark boxThe body that lets in only the light you want. The word comes from the Latin for room (camera)
02LensGathers more light to a point than a pinhole. Focal length sets the angle of view
03ApertureSize of the opening light passes through. Changes brightness and depth of field together
04ShutterHow long light comes in. Freezes motion or lets it flow
05Recording surfaceOn film, silver halide grains turn black to leave an image; on a sensor, pixels turn light into charge, stored as numbers
Camera history moved toward shorter exposures, smaller bodies and simpler printing

From darkroom to print
From silver gelatin prints to CMYK printing. Before digital, a chemical process stood between shooting and seeing. Screens add light; print subtracts it.
The darkroom — how exposed film becomes a photo on paper
① Negative and positiveThe negative (film), where bright things come out dark, is reversed again into a positive (photo paper)

④ Print developing — the image appearsAbout 1 minute in developer as the image darkens on the paper → stop → fix → wash
Figure 5 Darkroom work — from negative to positive. Before digital, developing and printing took more time than shooting.
Term
Negative — film whose exposed areas turn black, reversing light and dark. Projected onto photo paper again, it becomes a positive with the tones restored.

03FixDissolves unexposed silver so it no longer reacts

Lets you see what you are doing

One-page summary
12.1 Principles of perception
Motion is made not on the screen but in the viewer's perception. Making video is designing cognition.
12.4 · 12.10 Standards are conventions
24 frames, 16:9 and the 180-degree shutter are not laws of physics but the result of technical compromise and convention. Know the reasons and you can break them on purpose.
12.2 · 12.14 Viewing conditions and form
Just as the Kinetoscope created short attractions, the vertical screen created short-form.
12.3 · 12.11 Meaning between cuts
Meaning arises not within one cut but between two. A principle unchanged since Kuleshov.
12.4 · 12.8 New technology is a constraint first
New technology always arrives first as a constraint and only later becomes a means of expression. Generative AI is on the same path.
12.5 · 12.7 Smaller screen, bigger everything
As the screen shrinks, subjects get bigger, cuts get shorter and captions grow.
12.6 Nonlinear editing
Being able to revise endlessly makes you put off decisions. That is why a storyboard before shooting still matters.
12.12 · 12.13 From photography to print
A camera works on just five principles: box · lens · aperture · shutter · recording surface. Screens add light; print subtracts it.
Questions to consider
Explain why 24 frames became the standard, separating technical constraint from convention.
The technical constraint is the compromise between film consumption and continuity of motion; the convention is the 'cinematic feel' learned over the 100 years since.
Consider what way of viewing the video you are making now assumes, and how that assumption is changing its form.
Write on the first line of your proposal what device it will be watched on, where, and by how many people together, and the answers on length · shot size · captions follow.
Field tips
In meetings, don't describe a reference in words; send the link with the time range. Just writing "from 3:45 to 4:10" cuts meeting time in half.
When learning a new tool, first find out not its feature list but the existing process it replaces. Know its place and you learn faster.
If you don't know an industry term, ask on the spot. The term you pretended to know causes the biggest accidents.

The moment we turn on the camera, we make three decisions at once: where to stand, what to include and how much, and how long to show it. Together these decisions become meaning. What separates good video from bad is mostly not the gear but the precision of these decisions.

The language of video works like grammar. A close-up demands emotion; a long shot explains the situation. A low angle makes the subject big; a high angle makes it small. This is not taste but a convention audiences have learned over 100 years. Know the conventions and you can convey information without explanation; once you know them, you can also break them on purpose. Break rules you don't know and it just reads as a mistake.

Everything in this part can be practiced today, even without gear. Shooting one person in eight sizes on a single smartphone, and shooting the same conversation from two angles to compare: these are the real goals of this chapter. Knowing from reading and knowing from shooting are entirely different kinds of knowledge.
Shots, cuts and angles were not rules fixed from the start. Conventions early filmmakers discovered one by one, watching how audiences reacted, piled up into today's film grammar.

The Lumière brothers' first screenings in 1895 were mostly single-shot films from a fixed camera. The camera stayed in one place, like a seat at a play. In the same period, Georges Méliès used the trick of stopping the camera and starting it again to show that film could not only record reality but create a new one. Record and fantasy: these two branches live on today as documentary and VFX.

Telling a story by joining cuts developed fast in the early 1900s. Edwin Porter's The Great Train Robbery (1903) joined events in different places into a single chase. D. W. Griffith made systematic use of cross-cutting, close-ups that heighten emotion, and a rhythm that varies cut length with the pace of events. But his The Birth of a Nation (1915) is still sharply criticized for its racist content. Innovation in form does not guarantee the legitimacy of content.

Soviet filmmakers gave editing even more weight. Lev Kuleshov presented an experiment showing that when the same actor's blank face is joined to different scenes, audiences read entirely different emotions. Sergei Eisenstein argued that the collision of two cuts produces a new meaning found in neither, and divided montage into metric · rhythmic · tonal · intellectual montage. Today's ads that rapidly intercut a product with symbolic images stand on this tradition.

The Hollywood studio system, by contrast, chose editing that goes unnoticed. Rules that keep audiences from confusing space and time, like the 180-degree rule, eyeline match and match on action, were refined, and David Bordwell summed this up as the classical Hollywood style. Most of the continuity editing rules in this PART come from here.

In 1960, Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless deliberately broke these rules with jump cuts that skip time within the same framing. The jump cut, so common on YouTube today, was once revolutionary grammar. Film grammar is not a fixed code of law but a language audiences and makers have agreed on together, rewritten a little with every new platform.

How does the eye read the screen?

The rules of composition come from human visual perception before they are art-textbook conventions. Know how the viewer's eye moves, and composition stops being a formula to memorize and becomes a tool you can design with.

In the early 20th century, the German Gestalt psychologists Max Wertheimer · Wolfgang Köhler · Kurt Koffka argued that we don't add up parts to see a whole; we grasp the whole first. Things close together are seen as a group (proximity), similar things as belonging together (similarity), broken lines as continuous (continuity), and open shapes are completed as closed ones (closure). Put two people close together in frame and the audience reads them as being on the same side, no explanation needed.

In "Rubin's vase," introduced by Edgar Rubin in 1915, the same lines read as a vase or as two faces looking at each other. The eye makes only one thing the figure at a time. Controlling focus, brightness and color contrast in video is ultimately telling the audience what the figure is right now. Blurring the background with shallow depth of field and lighting only the person work on the same principle.

In Art and Visual Perception, Rudolf Arnheim described invisible forces at work in the frame. A rectangle's center, corners and diagonals hold a tension that pulls the eye, and the further an object strays from center, the less stable it feels. That balance of forces is why the rule of thirds feels comfortable and a figure pressed against the edge feels cramped. Composition is not finding the right answer but adjusting how much tension and stability there is.

In eye-tracking experiments in the 1960s, Alfred Yarbus showed that the eye moves over the same picture in entirely different ways depending on the question the observer is given. Asked to estimate the people's ages, observers look at faces; asked about their finances, at clothes and furniture. The audience's gaze follows not just shapes but the questions the story asks. Plant the question "who is coming in?" in one cut, and in the next the audience looks at the door first.

So composition and eye guidance can't be separated from editing. Put the next cut's key subject where the eye came to rest in the last, and the cut flows; put it deliberately on the opposite side, and you get a jolt. Whenever you meet a rule in this chapter, also ask: "where is the audience's eye right now?"

part03.html: A camera is a device that records light. How much light, for how long, and how sensitively? Understand these three and the order of operation is the same on any model. This PART answers the question "How do I shoot good video?" not with numbers but with an order of judgment.
Photo P-03 Aperture and focus rings on a cinema camera · generative image
P-03 Aperture and focus rings on a cinema camera
Understand the exposure triangle and set exposure manually
MaterialsMirrorless camera or smartphone pro mode, ND filter, light meter app
10 minIntroCompare the same scene shot in auto and in manual
15 minConceptsLock the shutter, set base ISO, direct with aperture. Why this order
10 minPlatesWalk through the frame-rate stack and the shutter-angle disc
10 minExerciseShoot one scene at F2.0 and at F8, log the adjustments
Check pointCan they explain what they locked first when changing exposure

A camera is a device that records light. Grasp this one sentence and the order of operation is the same on any model. How much light to let in, for how long, and how sensitively to receive it. Every other function supports these three.

The most common beginner mistake is leaving it all to auto. Auto exposure shifts brightness every time a cloud passes, and auto white balance gives each cut a different color. Footage is material that must cut together, so consistency comes before the polish of any single cut.

This part is full of numbers, but you don't need to memorize them. What you need is a feel for what you gain and lose when you turn each dial. Open the aperture and the background blurs, but focus misses rise; raise the sensitivity and the image brightens, but noise grows. Every choice has a price, and the DP is the one who knows the price and pays it.
Lens and eye — machine vision and human vision

The camera is often likened to the eye, but the two do not see the world the same way. The human eye sees sharply only in a tiny area called the fovea; the eyes dart about, and the brain stitches the fragments into one scene. That is why we feel we can see a bright window and a dark room equally well at once.

A camera sensor records the whole frame under the same conditions in one instant, so the view outside blows out to white or the interior sinks into black. We study exposure and dynamic range because the maker must now decide what the eye used to do automatically.

Focal length is also commonly misunderstood. Strictly speaking, what changes perspective is not focal length but the distance between camera and subject. To fill the frame with a face on a wide lens you must get close, and that distance makes the nose look big. To get the same size on a telephoto you must step far back, and that distance makes the background look close. Perspective is changed by the camera's position, not the lens.

'Normal lens' is also closer to a convention. A full-frame sensor's diagonal is about 43mm, so focal lengths near it are taken as closest to natural perspective, and by custom 50mm is called normal. What matters more than the number is whether the audience takes the scene as 'seeing it up close' or as 'peeking from afar'.

The f-number is the ratio of focal length to the diameter of the aperture opening. f/2 has a larger opening than f/4 and lets in four times the light, and the larger the opening, the shallower the depth of field. Depth of field also varies with focal length, subject distance and sensor size, so for a shallow look you can also move closer to the subject or put the background farther away. Technical terms form one connected system.

In the end, a camera is not a device that imitates the eye but one that shows the world in ways the eye cannot. It freezes 0.1 seconds, stretches 1 second into 10, and sees from impossible heights and distances. The numbers in this chapter are the language for using that new vision as you intend.
Further reading — Blain Brown, Cinematography: Theory and Practice · Gustavo Mercado, The Filmmaker's Eye
Every time gear got lighter, a new visual language was born. Ask first what the physical traits of the gear in your hands make possible.

There are only three ways to set image brightness, and each has its own price. The decisive difference from photography is that in video you can't use the shutter freely.

How many frames you split a second into sets the texture of motion; the shutter angle sets the motion blur. At 180°, the shutter speed is always double the frame rate.

Shutter angle is the angle over which the rotary shutter is open. Light enters for that share of each frame (1/24 s), and motion blurs by the same amount. Lighting and sound are the two most underrated areas, yet they shape the result more than anything. Viewers will sit through slightly soft footage to the end, but they leave muddy-sounding video within 3 seconds. An interview with a dark face reads as amateur work, however good the content.

Fortunately, in both areas understanding counts for more than money. A window and a white foam board solve half of portrait lighting, and bringing the mic to within 30 centimeters of the mouth removes most sound problems. Cheap gear up close always beats expensive gear far away.

This part covers not only how to add light but how to take it away. Half of low-key lighting is stealing light with black cloth, and half of good recording is switching off noise sources. Lighting design is not the craft of making things bright but of deciding where to leave dark.
An aesthetic history of light — from chiaroscuro to natural light

The language of film lighting began on painters' canvases. In late-16th-century Italy, Caravaggio painted dramatic scenes by revealing only part of a figure in strong light against darkness. Such strong light-dark contrast is called chiaroscuro, and its extreme form tenebrism. In 17th-century Holland, Rembrandt loved portraits in which light from one side leaves a small triangle on the shadowed cheek, and on today's sets this lighting bears his name.

The 1920 German Expressionist film The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari treated light and dark as a language of the psyche, even painting shadows directly onto the sets. With the emigration of German filmmakers in the 1930s–40s, this aesthetic crossed to Hollywood and carried into film noir's low-key lighting and venetian-blind shadows falling like prison bars. In 1949, DP John Alton described lighting in Painting with Light as a means of expression rather than a technique.

At the same time, the studio system set the standard for making stars look beautiful. Three-point lighting — key, fill, and backlight — became the formula for separating a person from the background and reliably modeling the face, and it is still the basis of interview and commercial shoots. Italian Neorealism and the French New Wave, by contrast, took light cameras and fast film into the streets, shooting in natural light and choosing realism over artificial beauty.

Today's DPs build their own language between these two traditions. Vittorio Storaro gave color and light symbolic meaning, while Roger Deakins is known for a naturalism that designs light around sources that could plausibly exist in the scene, such as windows or lamps. Digital sensors and LED lights let us shoot with less light, but the principles that govern direction, quality, and contrast have not changed.

When learning lighting, remember that every light has a motivation. Where does this light come from? Why this direction? What does the audience feel from it? The lighting patterns and gear in chapter 4 are tools for answering these questions.

We say we 'watch' video, but in fact we build one experience by seeing and hearing. In Audio-Vision (1990), the French composer and theorist Michel Chion proposed the idea of 'added value': when sound is added to an image, the audience mistakes its effect for the power of the image itself. The sound effect as a fist lands makes a far stronger impact than the real blow, yet the audience remembers the picture as intense. That is why good sound design goes unnoticed.

Chion also coined 'synchresis': the perceptual tendency to weld a sound and an image that occur together into one event. It's why a Foley artist can snap celery to make the sound of a breaking bone. Recording footsteps or the brush of a collar separately is called Foley after Jack Foley, who pioneered the field.

Sound divides into sound with a source inside the story world and sound without one. Radio music a character hears is inside the story; background music only the audience hears comes from outside it. The moment we learn that what we took for score is actually playing in a character's earphones, the audience steps into that character's inner world.

Editor and sound designer Walter Murch was credited as 'sound designer' on Apocalypse Now (1979), raising sound to a creative field with the same weight as cinematography or editing. He stressed designing the mix around the limit of how many overlapping layers of sound an audience can tell apart in one scene. Choosing what to keep matters more than putting a lot in.

In short-form and on mobile, many viewers watch with the sound off. The design has to work on captions and picture alone, yet for viewers with sound on, the first 1 second of sound can be the strongest hook. The mics and sound design of chapter 4 start from keeping both audiences in mind.

Shooting gathers material; editing makes meaning. Change the order and length and the same footage yields an entirely different video. Kuleshov proved this 100 years ago, and it works even harder in the short-form era of ever-shorter cuts.

This part starts from the history of editing technology and lays out Premiere Pro and After Effects features systematically. The feature lists are a map, not something to memorize. Know which area of which tool a problem belongs to and one search solves it; without a map, you wander for hours.

After Effects in particular thinks differently from Premiere. Premiere handles time horizontally; After Effects handles layers vertically. Trying to cut in After Effects without knowing this is the classic beginner's mistake. Simply splitting the two tools' roles halves your working time.
Good editing keeps the audience from noticing the editing. A cut slices time and space, yet the audience must feel it as a natural flow.

Editor Walter Murch's In the Blink of an Eye (1995) likens a blink to a cut. We blink when a thought changes or our gaze shifts. A good cut likewise falls where one paragraph of the viewer's thought ends. So the editor looks first not at the screen but at where the audience's mind has reached.

Murch ranked the criteria for a cut: emotion 51 percent, story 23 percent, rhythm 10 percent, eye-trace 7 percent, the 2D plane of the screen 5 percent, 3D spatial continuity 4 percent. The order matters more than the numbers: pick the cut with the right emotion even if continuity slips a little. Student work often flips this order, clinging to matched action and losing the emotional flow.

Continuity techniques — cutting on action, eyeline match, the 180-degree rule — all keep the audience from getting lost in space and time. Eisenstein's montage tradition did the opposite, exposing the seams to create collision and meaning. The editor chooses, case by case, to hide the seams or show them.

Editing is also an art of time. Shorter cuts raise tension; longer ones give the audience room to think. Cuts in ads and short-form speed up not just to pack in information but to keep catching the viewer's attention afresh.

Digital nonlinear editing made everything undoable, but it does not supply judgment. Even while learning the software, make a habit of asking at every cut, 'What is the audience feeling now?' Further reading: Walter Murch, In the Blink of an Eye; Ken Dancyger, The Technique of Film and Video Editing.

The illusion of life
— origins of the animation principles
How to breathe weight, character and emotion into still drawings was worked out over decades of trial and error. The principles of animation are physics and acting theory at once.

In 1914, Winsor McCay's Gertie the Dinosaur showed a character taking orders and reacting before an audience, proving animation could create a being with personality. Preparing Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the Walt Disney Studio had its animators observe real animals and people in motion and taught them drawing and anatomy.

Disney's core animators of the era were called the 'Nine Old Men.' Two of them, Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, distilled the studio's principles into twelve in The Illusion of Life (1981): squash and stretch, anticipation, staging, pose to pose, follow-through, slow in and slow out, arcs, secondary action, timing, exaggeration, solid drawing, appeal. These are less rules than ways of translating observed reality so the audience feels it more.

Half the principles are physics. A ball squashing as it lands and stretching as it bounces, a heavy object starting and stopping slowly — these make mass and inertia visible. The other half is acting. Anticipation signals the next action, exaggeration clarifies emotion, and appeal makes the audience give their heart to the character.

In 1987, Pixar's John Lasseter presented "Principles of Traditional Animation Applied to 3D Computer Animation" at SIGGRAPH. His point: the tools changed from pencil to computer, but how audiences sense life in motion did not. A motion designer easing a logo in the Graph Editor today follows the same principles.

Before memorizing the principles, build the habit of watching movement around you. An eye for the order in which a person rises from a chair or a ball rolls down stairs makes the principles living tools. Further reading: Frank Thomas · Ollie Johnston, The Illusion of Life; Richard Williams, The Animator's Survival Kit.

If you're still deciding on set, you're already late. A set burns hundreds of thousands of won an hour, and ten people wait on one person's decision. That is why professional sets are quiet: the decisions are already settled on paper.

Planning documents are not paperwork; they are a promise that no one will have to ask again on set. A storyboard is a device that makes ten people imagine the same frame, and the PPM is the procedure that locks every decision at the last moment when change is still cheap. In student projects too, gaps in understanding among team members must surface before the shoot day, not on it.

What I most want to stress is the one-sentence concept: this ad makes whom feel what, and in what way. If that sentence doesn't come, don't draw the storyboard. A plan that starts with pictures always collapses midway. Once the sentence is locked, everything follows from it: which cuts to drop, which music to choose, how many captions to use.
Archetypes of story — from the Poetics to the hero's journey

From a 15-second ad to a 90-minute film, stories that grip people share recurring structures. In the Poetics, Aristotle named plot, the arrangement of events, as the most important element of tragedy. A story must be a complete action with a beginning, middle and end, and its events must connect by necessity or probability. "Reversal," where a character's fortune turns, and "recognition," where an unknown truth comes to light, move the audience most. Today's twist-ending ads follow the same principle.

In 1863, the 19th-century German writer Gustav Freytag organized dramatic structure into five stages: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe. "Freytag's pyramid" describes a story as a curve of tension that rises and falls. In East Asia, gi-seung-jeon-gyeol, the four-part form born of the classical Chinese quatrain, has played a similar role. Because the direction changes at the third part, the "turn," it suits short videos especially well.

In the 20th century, the mythologist Joseph Campbell argued in The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) that myths around the world follow a similar journey: a hero leaves the ordinary world, undergoes trials and returns transformed. Christopher Vogler reworked this into a screenwriting method in The Writer's Journey, and Syd Field popularized 3-act structure and plot points in Screenplay (1979).

Use these structures as formulas and the story turns predictable. But understand why they work and you can use them differently. The audience enters a story when they know what the character wants, tenses up when that desire is blocked, and is moved when the character makes a choice. Make three things clear — desire, obstacle, choice — and the story lives, whether in four parts or 3 acts.

The same goes for brand films. The audience accepts a story when a person, not the product, is the protagonist, and the product is the helper that gets that person over the obstacle. The planning in this PART comes down to deciding whose desire, and which desire, to set before which obstacle.
Further reading: Aristotle, Poetics · Joseph Campbell, The Hero with a Thousand Faces · Robert McKee, Story

Design thinking and the language of feeling

Setting a world with adjectives may look like pure instinct, but it rests on methods long refined in design research and psychology. In The Sciences of the Artificial (1969), Herbert Simon defined design as "action that turns the current state into a better one," widening it from a branch of art into a method of problem solving. Later, IDEO and the Stanford d.school popularized the stages of empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test, and the term "design thinking" came into wide use.

The classic study using adjectives as a measuring tool is psychologist Charles Osgood's semantic differential. In The Measurement of Meaning (1957), he had people score their impressions on pairs of opposite adjectives such as "good-bad," "strong-weak," and "fast-slow." Placing adjectives on sensory axes in section 2.13 applies exactly this principle.

In the 1970s the Japanese engineer Mitsuo Nagamachi systematized "Kansei engineering," which gathers users' feelings about a product as adjectives and turns them into concrete design elements. It translates the vague sense of a "sporty car" into design values such as body lines, seat height, and dashboard color. The tone-and-manner chart, which turns adjectives into color, light, lens, and cutting pace in video, has the same structure.

The adjective method is especially useful because it aligns the team's language. The director's "warm," the DP's "warm," and the editor's "warm" can all differ. A mood board and a tone-and-manner chart bring these differences out before the shoot and get the team to agree. Ask first-time viewers of the finished piece which adjectives come to mind, and you can check whether the intended world came through.

Design thinking, in the end, is refusing to leave creativity to chance and making it a repeated cycle of observation, definition, and experiment. Three adjectives are where that cycle starts and where you return when lost.

When the screen is not a rectangle, when the audience walks instead of sitting, the rules of planning change at the root. 360-degree video has no frame, an exhibition has no pause button, and an outdoor ad has no sound. Carry conventional film grammar into these conditions unchanged, and you will fail.

Still, the principles carry over. Without a frame you must still guide the eye; with a walking audience you must still design rhythm; without sound you still need dynamics. Only the means change: light and sound draw the eye instead of framing, the visitor's path makes rhythm instead of cuts, and contrast makes dynamics instead of music.

Specs are a search away, but little has been written on how a person in a cinema seat and a person scrolling on the subway take in the same video differently. Knowing that difference is a planner's real edge.
A history of screens and the audience's body

Where audiences watch has moved from the theater seat to the living-room sofa, to the screen in the palm, and into devices worn on the head. Each time the screen changed, so did the grammar of the moving image.

In the late 18th century the British painter Robert Barker introduced the "panorama," wrapping the entire wall of a round building in a landscape painting. Viewers stood at the center and took in cities and battlefields spread across 360 degrees. The desire to step into a picture is older than film; today's 360 video and immersive exhibitions are its latest form.

As television entered homes, the film industry widened the screen to stress an experience only theaters could give. The result was Cinerama and CinemaScope in the 1950s, and IMAX, first shown at the 1970 Osaka Expo. With wider screens, directors developed compositions that set a character to one side and let landscape and empty space carry the emotion.

Change also ran the other way. Morton Heilig's 1962 "Sensorama" added vibration, wind, and smell to film, and in 1968 Ivan Sutherland showed an early head-mounted display. Here the audience is no longer looking at a screen but standing inside it. When the medium changes, the audience's body changes; when the body changes, the grammar changes.

The smartphone made the screen small again, and vertical. On a screen held in one hand, the human face becomes the key subject, and captions and interface become part of the image. As Marshall McLuhan said in Understanding Media (1964), "the medium is the message": the same content is received differently depending on the medium that carries it.

The body responds differently to different screen sizes. In a theater the screen fills most of the field of view, so wide landscapes and a slow pace work; a vertical screen in the hand fills only part of it, and the viewer can flick to the next video at any moment. So if you change only the aspect ratio, the rhythm collapses. Cut length, information density, even the size of the figures must be redesigned.

Sound conditions differ too. A theater assumes multichannel sound and low noise; a phone means a small speaker or earphones, and in public people watch muted. Outdoor LED and in-store signage should be assumed to have no sound at all. That is why captions and graphics become the main carriers. Behind every number in a spec table, picture the audience's posture and surroundings.
Further reading — Marshall McLuhan, Understanding Media · Lev Manovich, The Language of New Media · Anne Friedberg, The Virtual Window

Before working with immersive content, we should be clear about what it means for an audience to feel "inside" it. Immersion is a matter of conditions, not image quality.

The history of immersive technology begins with attempts to enlarge the screen. In the 1950s Cinerama filled a curved screen with three projectors to cover even peripheral vision, followed by CinemaScope and 70mm film. Heilig's 1962 Sensorama added vibration, wind, and even smell, and Sutherland's 1968 head-mounted display was so heavy it had to hang from the ceiling, earning the nickname "the Sword of Damocles." The goal was always the same: to pull the audience's vision and senses as far toward the screen as possible.

Researchers split this experience into two concepts. Immersion is the objective condition that equipment and content provide: field of view, response speed to head movement, directionality of sound. Presence is the subjective state the user actually feels, the sense that "I am here." With the same equipment, presence varies greatly with content design. That is why an expensive headset can still deliver a flat experience.

The most common presence-breakers are latency and mismatch. When the image lags a turn of the head, the brain detects a gap between the motion the eyes see and the motion the vestibular system feels. This is the main cause of cybersickness. So VR production keeps frame rates high, avoids camera moves the user did not make, and uses mitigations such as vignetting that masks the edges of the view. Stability comes before image quality.

The premises of directing change too. In 360 video and VR the audience can look anywhere, so the director has only means to guide, not to force. The direction a sound comes from, differences in brightness, a character's gaze and movement, and the layout of the space turn the viewer's head. To keep viewers from missing a key event, plant cues before it happens.

In AR and projection mapping the image sits on real space, so actual light levels, surface materials, and where the audience stands decide the result. A dark wall in an indoor gallery and a building facade at midday are entirely different media. The quality of immersive content is decided not by the final file but by the place where it will be shown.
Further reading — Mel Slater, "A Note on Presence Terminology" · Jaron Lanier, Dawn of the New Everything · Jason Jerald, The VR Book

Second, voice comes first. Glasses are a hands-free medium, so a flow of asking and answering replaces touch. Third, 1st-person video becomes the default format. Every head movement is captured, and aspect ratios vary by device, so you can't assume horizontal 16:9.

Museums are where MR is most convincing, because the constraint that originals cannot be touched or moved becomes MR's very strength.

The National Museum of Korea runs a digital immersive gallery within its permanent exhibition, showing content such as a VR Goguryeo mural tomb, large panoramic films, and a digital Gwanggaeto Stele, and major national museums abroad also run artifact-restoration AR and MR tours. Their setups mostly come down to three elements.

Restoration holograms — the missing shards of broken pottery, or a worn Buddha statue's original colors, laid over the real object. Keep some transparency so the line between original and restoration shows.
Docent avatars — read the visitor's gaze and position to explain the artifact they are looking at. Keep the talk under 30 seconds per artifact; the visitor chooses whether to hear more.
Hand-tracking control — pick up, turn, and enlarge artifacts by hand, without controllers. Place objects within arm's reach (about 0.5–0.7 m) and have them return to place when handling ends.

The point starts at 0D, so volume is 3D and adding time makes 4D. Remember that point, line, plane, volume, time each add one motion, in that order, and you won't get confused.

In geometry, a point has position but no size and is 0D; a line, the path of a moving point, is 1D; a plane, the path of a moving line, is 2D; and a volume, the path of a moving plane, is 3D. Add time and it becomes 4D, and when the viewer walks inside, movement through place is added.

0PointA single light in the dark, a single particle. The strongest device for drawing the eye to one spot
1LineLight trails, lasers, LED lines. They show direction and speed and guide movement
2PlaneScreens, walls, floors, translucent scrims. Projection mapping turns a building's planes into screens
3VolumeVolumetric lighting, hologram effects, anamorphic illusion. Make volume appear on a plane or create it in the air
4TimeChange and motion. The same space becomes an entirely different scene over time
+Moving through placeThe scene changes as visitors walk. Film moves place with cuts; in immersive space, the visitor's body moves place
The more video moves from the flat plane into space, the more the planner designs the viewer's position instead of the camera's.<small>6.14 Video is space-time in motion</small>
Video records 3D space on a 2D screen and adds time to set it in motion. Editing cuts and joins that space-time (1.20); immersive content brings the viewer's body inside it.

How do you make an ad work and imprint a brand? The audience didn't come to watch ads. Learn the structure that wins attention, understanding and memory under these hostile conditions, and take apart the techniques of directors and production companies by asking why they did it that way.

Advertising is the hardest form: it must move a stranger's heart in a very short time. The audience didn't come for the ad, and most are waiting for it to end. Having to leave something behind under these hostile conditions is what sets advertising apart from other video.

So advertising has a strict structure: grab attention, make it understood, make it remembered. In 15 seconds, these three stages get 3, 8 and 4 seconds. There must be one message; put in two and both vanish. This is not taste but a rule of thumb proven again and again.

The second half of this PART analyzes the techniques of directors and production companies. Not to copy them, but to understand why they did what they did. Learning starts the moment you pause an ad you like and write down why it cut here. Hitting like is not research.
An ad's goal is not admiration in the moment of viewing but a memory that surfaces when it's needed. Designing an ad film is, in the end, designing the audience's attention and memory.

One of the oldest models is AIDA, credited to the American adman Elias St. Elmo Lewis in the late 19th century: attention, interest, desire, action. Many object that consumers don't follow these steps in order, but one point still holds: in a short ad, if you don't win attention first, the other stages never begin.

On memory, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve is often cited. His experiments in the 1880s showed that newly learned information fades fast, but repetition slows the forgetting. That is why ads are repeated across many media. The mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc described in 1968, the tendency to like what we see often, belongs to the same picture.

In How Brands Grow (2010), marketing scholar Byron Sharp described the key to brand growth as 'mental availability': how easily a brand comes to mind in a buying situation. Distinctive assets such as color, logo, sound, character and slogan must be repeated consistently, and the brand clearly linked within the ad. If an ad was fun but nobody remembers whose it was, it may have helped another brand.

Daniel Kahneman described human thinking as a fast, intuitive System 1 and a slow, analytical System 2. Short video ads work mostly on System 1: viewers take them in through feeling and impression rather than logic. The 'peak-end rule', that the most intense moment and the last moment of an experience shape the whole memory, is a good guide for designing an ad's climax and ending.

The hooks, message design, structures by length and brand imprinting in this chapter all rest on these principles of memory. When planning an ad, ask 'what will stay in the viewer's head a week later?' before 'what should we show?' Further reading — Byron Sharp, How Brands Grow; Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow; Robert Cialdini, Influence.

An ad is persuasion, not a story. Even when it uses narrative, the narrative serves persuasion, and the structure always passes through three stages: attention, understanding, memory.

Borrowing is not making. Copyright is not a rule to block creation but a social contract to keep it going. Copyright protects expression, not ideas. This is the idea-expression dichotomy. The idea of 'a story that turns back time' is open to anyone, but a specific work's dialogue, scene construction, and editing rhythm belong to that work. To use a reference means to learn its principles, not to copy its frames.

Korean copyright law separates economic rights from moral rights. Economic rights cover reproduction, performance, public transmission, distribution, the making of derivative works, and more, and they can be transferred. Moral rights, such as the right of attribution and the right of integrity, stay with the creator and cannot be transferred. A commissioning contract may say 'all rights are transferred' and moral rights still remain, so in practice a separate agreement not to exercise them is common.

Video stacks several layers of rights. To use one song, you must clear both the copyright in the music and lyrics and the neighboring rights in the recording. 'I bought the track' usually means a license to play it, which is not the right to put it in a video. Performers' faces and voices carry likeness rights and publicity interests, and a location may need the facility manager's consent. Fonts, logos, even a poster that happens to land in the background can be subject to rights.

Fair use is the clause that handles exceptions. Article 35-5 of the Korean Copyright Act provides that, for uses such as reporting, criticism, education, and research, the purpose and character of the use, the type of work, the share of the work used, and the effect on the market be weighed together. It is not an automatic exemption but a standard judged after the fact. The folk rule that 'up to a few seconds is fine' has no basis. Quote only as much as you need, cite the source, and do not replace the original's market.

Generative AI adds new questions. The legality of training data, the authorship of outputs, and outputs that imitate a particular creator's style are under debate in many countries. Many countries, Korea included, have taken the position that output without human creative contribution can hardly be copyrighted. Make a habit of recording the tools and prompts you used and the extent of human involvement. In this book's plates, too, the diagrams were designed by the author, while the figure drawings and reference images were made with generative AI; the terms are set out in the appendix.

Three habits protect your practice. First, record the source and scope of use for every asset you use. Second, check the contract for the scope, term, media, and territory of the rights. Third, if in doubt, don't use it, or ask permission. Most copyright disputes start not from malice but from missing records. Further reading — Korea Copyright Commission, Copyright Made Easy: 100 Consultation Cases; Copyright Act, Article 35-5; Lawrence Lessig, Free Culture.

New equipment has always produced new images. Here are five such moments. The first is sound. After "The Jazz Singer" in 1927, as sync sound became standard, the noisy camera was shut away in a soundproof booth, and early talkies actually turned visually stiff. Only after the blimp and the boom mic were developed could the camera move again. This order, in which a new technology first constrains expression and later frees it, would repeat from then on.

The second is film speed and lenses. Deep-focus shooting in the 1940s required stopping down for a deep depth of field, which in turn demanded a lot of light and fast film stock. That figures in front and behind are sharp at once in "Citizen Kane" was both an aesthetic choice and a result of technology. The audience chooses where to look, and the characters' relationships are revealed through composition.

The third is the lighter camera. As portable sync-sound equipment spread in the late 1950s, cinéma vérité in France and direct cinema in the US emerged. Once the camera went out into the streets, shaky frames and improvised compositions began to read as the mark of the real. The handheld look of today's variety shows and vlogs inherits that convention.

The fourth is the digital intermediate and color grading. In the early 2000s, as the process of scanning film to digital, grading it, and transferring it back to film took hold, it became possible to redesign a whole scene's color in post-production. This is where color became a work's signature, as with teal-and-orange contrast. Today it is common to set the look at the shooting stage and apply it to the monitors on set.

The fifth is the smartphone and the vertical screen. As shooting, editing, and distribution came to be done on one device, production cycles shortened, and the vertical frame made people-centered close-ups and fast cuts the default. Captions stand in for sound, and the first 3 seconds govern the whole structure. It is not that the aspect ratio changed; the audience's viewing posture and setting changed.

There is a common lesson. Technology does not decide form, but it changes the range of what is possible. Those who explore that range first create the grammar of the next generation. When you read a case, ask not only 'what was used?' but also 'what did that equipment make possible?' Making a good video and getting it discovered are different skills. Since YouTube removed the barriers to distribution, the starting point of planning has moved from the idea to discoverability. That is why titles and thumbnails have become part of directing.

Each platform has its own grammar. YouTube runs on search and watch time, Instagram on saves and shares, TikTok on participation and derivative works. Posting the same video unchanged and then remarking that results differ only shows you don't know what each platform rewards.

This part covers everything from writing titles to building hashtags, answering comments, interpreting performance metrics and the basics of running ads. Why does a maker need this? Because the role most in demand in today's job market is the person who makes, posts and reads the numbers.
The attention economy and the algorithmic audience

In the platform era, video does not go straight to the audience; it arrives via recommendation algorithms. To understand views, you must first understand a scarce resource: attention. In a 1971 talk Herbert Simon said that 'a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,' and in the late 1990s Michael Goldhaber and others called this situation the 'attention economy.' Today every video competes for a few seconds of people's time on the same screen.

Platforms leave the refereeing of this competition to algorithms. In 2012 YouTube announced it would shift its recommendation criteria from clicks to watch time, and since then many platforms have weighted behavioral signals such as retention, completion rate, rewatches and shares. The workings are not public and change often, but the principle is clear: videos that people watch to the end, watch again and send to others get shown to more people.

There are two lessons for makers. First, even if the thumbnail and title win the click, retention drops and recommendations shrink when the content breaks the promise. Exaggerated titles gain short-term clicks and lose long-term trust. Second, what matters is the loop of checking drop-off points, early and midway, in the data and applying what you learn to the next video. The metrics reading in chapter 9 is a tool for this loop.

There is a common structure too. The system first shows a video to a small group of users as a test, then widens or narrows its reach based on the response. The signals it reads are how long people watched and whether to the end, whether they saved or shared it, and whether they came back. Views are a result, not a cause. The variables a maker can work with are not views but retention and response rates.

There is one trap. The observation that a metric breaks down once it becomes a target is known as Goodhart's law. Sensational thumbnails and exaggerated titles raise short-term CTR but increase drop-off and erode trust in the whole channel. Metrics are a window onto the audience's response, not the audience itself.

In the algorithm era, the maker's responsibility grows too. Disinformation, violating other people's portrait rights, and passing off generative-AI images as real are not worth any number of short-term views. A good channel does not trick the algorithm; it steadily gives value to a specific audience. In the end, the algorithm follows the behavior of the people who find that value.
Further reading — Tim Wu, The Attention Merchants · Michael Goldhaber, "The Attention Economy and the Net"

Before comparing tools, we first map where this technology enters the production process. Generative AI for video has grown along three branches: models that make images from text, video models that make motion from images and text, and audio models that make voices and music. Their roots differ, but they work in similar ways. They learn patterns from vast amounts of data, then produce results that fit the given conditions probabilistically. That is why the same prompt gives a different result every time.

In practice this probabilistic nature shows up in two ways: drafts come very fast, and the same result is hard to get twice. So in the field, AI serves less as the maker of final output than as a tool for early exploration. It suits stages where you need to see many options fast: rough storyboard images, concept art, layout drafts, caption drafts, alternative copy.

Consistency is the biggest challenge. The same character's face shifts slightly from scene to scene, and the lighting in the same space changes from cut to cut. Fixes include feeding in reference images, making a key image first and generating the rest to match it, and correcting in post-production. Decide in advance 'how far AI goes and where people take over,' or the schedule will fall apart.

In the end, the yardstick is problem-solving. AI quickly produces results that are plausible on average, but it cannot answer why this brand must say this message now, or what the audience should feel in this scene. Judgments of planning, structure and taste still belong to people. The cheaper the tools get, the more the difference lies in the questions of the person using them.

Ethical and legal questions follow too. The source of training data, imitating a particular artist's style, and synthesizing a real person's face or voice all need careful handling. On a commercial project, check the terms of use for whether commercial use is allowed and who owns the rights, and tell the client in advance how far AI will be used. When you use a person's face or voice, always get that person's consent.

In short, this technology does not remove a stage of production; it sharply lowers the cost of a first draft at every stage. What grows is not slack but options. The skilled people of this era are those who know what to choose from a bigger pile of drafts.

Video makes a fine hobby, but most readers of this book want to work in it. Then you need to understand the market's structure first. Knowing where the money flows, who gives work to whom, and which jobs are growing and which are shrinking is part of the skill.

The change to watch is that the center of gravity of video jobs has moved from broadcasting and film to digital, commerce and in-house corporate teams. Broadcasters' open recruitment was once the only gateway; now brand content teams, e-commerce companies' video staff and small studios hire far more newcomers. This shift has changed what goes into a portfolio, too.

Meanwhile, generative AI is driving down the rates for simple editing and simple graphics. The way to survive is not learning tools faster but moving up into judgment. Deciding what to shoot, explaining why this cut, and reaching agreement with the client are still human work.
Where the value of video comes from

Many people and companies are involved before a video reaches its audience. Know where in that chain value is created, and you will see where you can stand. The traditional film industry was divided into development and financing, production, distribution and exhibition; after the theatrical release, a film came out in turn on video, pay TV and free-to-air broadcast. Staggering release dates by medium is called holdback, or windowing. It was a structure for earning from different audiences with the same work.

Streaming services shook this order hard. Works now skip theaters and go straight out worldwide, and more platforms finance and produce directly. YouTube and short-form platforms opened a way for individual creators to skip financing and distribution and meet audiences directly. As production costs fall and distribution barriers disappear, the value of video is shifting more and more to 'who can gather an audience.'

A key concept in this shift is intellectual property, or IP. When one story and its characters expand from webtoon to drama, games and merchandise, the value multiplies. Korean content draws attention worldwide not just through individual hits but through the power of its stories, characters and worlds to carry over into other media.

Seen from the production floor, value doesn't come from technical skill alone. An ad's value comes from solving the brand's problem, an educational video's from helping learners understand, a creator video's from trust with a particular audience. When two people with the same shooting skills command different fees, the reason is usually this difference in problem-solving.

A useful frame for looking at the industry is the value chain. Ask who bears the risk and who takes the profit at each stage: planning and development, production, post-production, distribution, exhibition and consumption. Traditionally, investors and production companies bore the risk, and profit was recouped in distribution and exhibition. In the platform era, much of the risk has shifted to the platforms; in exchange, more production companies take a stable production fee and give up extra earnings tied to performance.

An individual creator's income comes in four streams: commissioned freelance work, a share of platform ad revenue, direct brand partnerships, and your own business, such as products and teaching. The earlier streams are predictable; the later ones swing widely but have a higher ceiling. Rely on just one and you will be shaken when the market shifts, so it is safer to try at least two from early in your career.

The figure on a quote is not simply the cost of the gear, nor of the hours. A production budget usually splits into three blocks: people's time, equipment and locations, and rights. Beginners most often forget the third. The same video is priced differently for 1 year of in-house training than for 6 months on national TV. The wider the media, term, and territory, the higher the price, and if the quote leaves the scope unstated, the work can end up used without limit.

People's time is not just the shoot day. A project runs from planning meetings and research, script and storyboard, casting and scouting, and the shoot, through editing and revisions, to delivery and invoicing. The less experienced you are, the less time you allow for editing and revisions, yet that is where the most time disappears. The standard defense is a clause that fixes the number of revisions and bills anything beyond as extra.

There are three ways to set a price: hours times an hourly rate, the going rate for similar projects, or the value the client gains. As your career grows, the third carries more weight, because even at the same 30 seconds, a small shop's intro video and the main cut of a national campaign solve problems of very different size. You can price this way only if you can explain what problem your work solves.

In Korea, the standard contracts and industry surveys published by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), and others serve as benchmarks. A standard contract covers payment timing, copyright ownership, scope of revisions, and termination terms, which makes it a good skeleton for a first contract. Amounts change every year, so check the latest figures, but the structure of the items changes little.

Finally, a low price does not bring the next job. Start too cheap and it gets hard to refuse revision requests, and that time is lost to other work. You may take a low fee early on for the experience, but even then, write down the scope and number of revisions clearly. Guarding your price is guarding your time.
Further reading — KOCCA, standard contracts and industry surveys · Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, standard contracts for popular culture and arts · Chris Do, “Sell Value, Not Price”
