Skill is only skill once it's proven. However well you make something, if you keep it in a form you can't show, it might as well not exist. This part covers the craft of proof.

A recruiter spends 1 to 2 minutes on a portfolio on average. In that short time, they want to know just one thing: if we give this person the work, will they see it through? One finished piece answers that better than one flashy cut. Few applicants submit their proposal and storyboard with the work, so simply showing the process sets you well apart.

The same logic is why interviews and communication get their own sections. Video work looks solitary, but it is really a job of coordinating all day long. The habits of repeating instructions back, sharing progress first, and reporting mistakes immediately are judged before technique. Most of what gets you through your first 3 months at your first job lies here too.

Video tools change every few years. The menus of the software you are learning now may well change by the time you graduate. The American radio host Ira Glass has spoken of the 'taste gap' that people starting out in creative work go through. When you start, your taste is already good enough to recognize good work, but your hands can't yet keep up. The only way to close the gap is to keep turning out a large volume of work.

Tool skills matter, but what recruiters and clients finally look at is judgment. Someone who can explain which cuts they dropped, why they chose this angle, and what they prioritized within the deadline and budget adapts quickly when the tools change. That is why a portfolio should hold not just the work but the process and the reasons for your choices.

Video is almost always made collaboratively. The DP, editor, sound designer, client, and actors each speak their own language. A good video maker can translate their intent into other people's language, and takes feedback as information, not emotion. Meeting deadlines, organizing files, and replying when promised: these basics bring the next job.

And what remains in the end is perspective. Given the same tools and the same place, each person sees something different and wants to say something different. In an age when generative AI produces images with ease, this difference matters even more. Anyone can borrow technology, but no one can borrow the ability to judge what is good and say why you are making it.

A useful concept for the first few years of a career is 'T-shaped expertise.' The vertical stroke is the strength to go deep in one field; the horizontal stroke is the breadth to understand neighboring fields and collaborate. An editor who knows the limits of shooting can judge what extra footage to ask for on set, and a DP who knows how the edit flows secures the needed cuts in advance. What a newcomer needs is to do one thing well while understanding the fields beside it.

Remember, too, how to handle feedback. As a beginner, it's easy to take criticism of your work as a judgment of you. But feedback on set is usually information about the output, and the sooner you get information, the better. People who can explain 'why I did it this way' and ask 'what to change, and how' grow far faster in the same time. The hands-on preparation in chapter 11 is, in the end, practice in this attitude.
Further reading — Austin Kleon, “Steal Like an Artist” · David Bayles · Ted Orland, “Art and Fear”

A portfolio is not a collection of well-made videos but a bundle of evidence showing what problems you solve and how. Recruiters do not spend long on a showreel. Surveys and field experience agree that whether they keep watching is decided within the first 10 to 20 seconds. Ordering work chronologically or saving your best for later almost always costs you.

According to the serial position effect in cognitive psychology, people remember the beginning and end of a list best. Portfolios follow the same principle. Open with strong work, show range in the middle, and close with strong work again. Padding with ordinary work to add volume lowers the average. A portfolio is judged by impression, not by sum.

What to show depends on the role. Camera applicants must prove light and composition; editing applicants, rhythm and structure. From the same project, pick the passages that reveal transitions and pacing for an editing role, and the scenes that show lighting design for a camera role. Applying to every role with one showreel is like wearing an outfit that fits no occasion.

Showing the process makes the decisive difference. Note briefly your intent, references, storyboard, the constraints on set, and the choices you made within them, and reviewers will read the judgment behind the result. Stories of handling limits, such as a scene solved with natural light for lack of budget or an edit restructured because the schedule slipped, leave an especially strong impression.

Stating your contribution accurately is both ethics and strategy. Clearly noting your part in team work earns trust and makes interview answers easier. Inflated contributions usually come out after one or two specific questions. Even for school or personal projects, if you used commercial assets or music without permission, it is safer to keep them out of a public portfolio.

Finally, a portfolio is not an object you finish but a state you keep updating. Set yourself a rule to drop the weakest piece whenever a new one arrives, and the average keeps rising even if the volume doesn't.

What will you say? This book has spent hundreds of pages on technique, but one sentence should remain at the end: an editing tool is only a tool.

Software changes its interface within 3 years, and within 5 a new tool replaces the standard. The shortcuts you know by heart today will be strange relics to the next generation. Generative AI has made this distinction sharper. The cheaper it gets to make a plausible image, the more valuable the person who can say why it must be this image. Having something to say has become harder than learning tools fast.
The thesis this book has carried throughout

The age of the one-person company
And the power of culture. Creators no longer just make work; they run themselves as a business. And the accumulation of that skill becomes the power of culture.

Long ago, Lee O-young said an age was coming when each individual would become a company. Then it was a metaphor; now it is a description. Planning, shooting and editing on one smartphone and distributing worldwide is now a reality. That is why this book covers not only planning and production but platform management, reading results, contracts and careers.

In Baekbeom Ilji, Kim Gu wrote that what he wanted was not a rich and powerful nation but one with a high power of culture, because the power of culture makes us happy and brings happiness to others. It was a bold declaration, setting culture as a national goal at a time with neither military nor economic might.
This is not the achievement of a few geniuses. It is the accumulated skill of tens of thousands, and that skill begins with education.

Korean video content now stands where that sentence has come true. It wins at Cannes and the Academy Awards, sets global streaming viewing records, and its fusion of music and video has become one of the world's standards. The readers of this book will supply that skill for the next generation. Getting exposure right, recording clean sound, cutting for a reason, meeting deadlines. That accumulation becomes the power of culture.

Background 22
What gets expensive when tools get cheap

In 1965, Intel co-founder Gordon Moore published his observation that the number of components on an integrated circuit doubles at regular intervals. What matters in this rule of thumb, known as Moore's law, is not the number but the consequence. When a resource keeps getting cheaper, people change how they work so as to use it freely. Economists describe this as complements rising in value. When one thing gets cheap, what is used alongside it becomes more valuable.

For the past 100 years, the most expensive thing in video production was 'the cost of one more take.' Every foot of film, every day of cast and crew, cost money. So every production practice, from storyboards to rehearsals to test shoots, was designed to reduce failure. When digital shooting eliminated the cost of film, the first thing to change on set was the number of takes.

Generative tools go one step further. The cost of making a draft has fallen close to 0. Getting three concept images once meant days of an illustrator's time, so you thought long about which three to ask for. Now you can see 100 in 30 minutes. The hard thinking has moved from 'what to ask for' to 'what to choose.'

So what got expensive? First, judgment. The ability to tell which of 100 images fits the brand and will work for the audience cannot be generated. Second, trust. When anyone can make a plausible image, what clients pay for is not the image but the assurance that 'hand it to this person and it gets done, responsibly.' Third, the real thing. The value of shooting what cannot be generated, such as real products, real stores and real people's faces, has actually gone up.

Knowing this structure also makes clear where students should spend their time. You can learn to operate a tool in a few days. But the ability to say why a cut works, the trust that comes from meeting deadlines and the eye that reads light on set respond only to accumulation. There is one yardstick for reading the numbers in the sections ahead: what did this change make cheap, and so what did it make valuable?
Further reading — Carl Shapiro · Hal Varian, Information Rules · Erik Brynjolfsson · Andrew McAfee, The Second Machine Age · Ethan Mollick, Co-Intelligence

PART 12Practice and careers in the AI transition
People, digital doubles, consent

AI actors, digital doubles and the question of consent. Generative tools proved useful fastest with backgrounds and props; the area that stays hard longest is people. Because audiences have trained all their lives to read faces, people are a technical problem and a rights problem at once.
P12-MOCAP Digital doubleAn actor in a marker-covered motion capture suit, performing surrounded by cameras
NoteDigital double — scan a real actor and record their movement. Consent and a usage-scope contract come first
Motion capture — from the studio down to one phone
Optical markers — studio · sports scienceDozens of infrared cameras + reflective markers. Millimeter precision; the standard in sports-science motion labs and big VFX. Needs space

The best reference image is a single front view with flat lighting and a neutral expression. The more distinctive features, the harder they are to hold.
Keeping the same face
A face that changes from cut to cut is the most common failure. In practice, you make the reference first and match everything else to it.
01Reference imageLock one front view first
02Reference inputFeed the reference into every later generation; prompt only the angle · lighting · pose

Rights: four things to check first
01Likeness — using a real person's face · voice · signature gestures requires their consent. Creating a look-alike can also be a problem.
02Scope — specify media · term · territory · extent of edits. 'Consent to be filmed' and 'consent to AI training and generation' are separate items.
03Disclosure — when a generated person is shown as if real, it is safest to label it so no one is misled.
04Records — keep the model used, the prompts, and the sources of reference images. Disputes usually escalate when there are no records.

Sets, LED walls, generated backgrounds

From sets to LED walls, and on to generated backgrounds. In 100 years the way backgrounds are made has changed three times: build it or go there, put an image up behind, or composite it in post-production. Generative tools have sharply cut the cost of the third and changed how material for the second is made.

Bringing in a whole space

Shooting a real space in many photos or clips, rebuilding it as 3D data, then moving the camera freely inside it has entered everyday practice. Photogrammetry has been joined by methods that learn and reproduce even the brightness of light rays, so subjects that were hard to rebuild, like glass · metal · foliage, are now workable. Shoot a store for half a day and every later ad can be shot in that space: the shoot itself becomes an asset.
Saying you will decide the background later means saying you will decide the lighting later. The background comes first.<small>11.5 Sets, LED walls, generated backgrounds</small>

Elements and particles

Why is simulation still here? Generative models are good at 'motion they have seen often,' but water pouring, cloth draping and smoke curling along a wall are still unstable. These are the results of physical laws, and a generative model does not calculate laws; it makes pictures that look similar.

NoteSimulation — change one variable and recalculate; the same settings give the same result

Aspect

Brand assets may not be distorted. In a cut of a drink being poured into a glass, if the label warps for even one frame, the cut is unusable.

When the product is the hero — no distortion of label or shape is allowed.
Repeat delivery — when one scene ships in versions for many countries, a different result every time means no control.
Exact timing — a request like a droplet landing at 0.4 seconds to hit the music can only be met by calculation.

Student vision and expertise

What vision and expertise should students have? There is no answer to 'what should I learn to be safe.' Knowing how to operate a tool goes stale in 2–3 years at most. The better question is 'what abilities hold their value whatever changes.'

NoteStarting up — when the entrance narrows, becoming your own client is also a career path

Generative tools produce averagely plausible results very fast. So the value of average output quickly converges to 0, and what rises in value is judgment that departs from the average: the ability to explain 'why it has to be this.'
Four things that hold their value
<small>Problem definition</small>Translate symptoms into causes
Turn 'make us a video' into 'we need more first visits from new customers'
<small>Grounds for judgment</small>Why this one out of ten
Ten drafts take a few minutes
Whoever can say why they chose becomes the one in charge
<small>Feel for the real</small>An eye for the lies in generated images
Cuts with mismatched shadow directions, cuts whose depth of field can't be explained
Only people who have set lights and swapped lenses catch them
<small>Language skills</small>Proposals · director's notes · feedback · prompts
Writing the picture in your head so people and machines understand it the same way is productivity itself
Term

Broom-shaped — the T-shape (deep in one thing, understanding adjacent fields) with a wider crossbar. Think of an editor who also handles motion graphics · sound cleanup · thumbnails, or a DP who also proposes a rough cut and color-correction standards.
The shape of expertise: from T to broom

As AI tools lower the barriers to adjacent fields, the broom shape with its wider crossbar has become the realistic model. But a wider crossbar does not make the vertical stroke unnecessary. Someone who does everything passably ends up competing with tools that do everything passably. Pick one field you can answer for, and be able to show its depth as evidence.

Evidence — finished output
Collaboration — communicating within your stage

Tools — how fast you switch tools and why you choose them

Don't be afraid. You have already done plenty.

Key message and copy

Where does the emotional punch come from? After a good ad, what people remember is not the image but one sentence. The more easily generative tools make images, the more a work's level depends on whether it has a sentence to drive home.
A key message is a choice, not a summary
A key message means dropping nine of the ten things you could say and keeping just one. If dropping them hurts, it isn't decided yet. Test it three ways.
01One-sentence rule — it must finish as one sentence with no conjunctions. If 'and' or 'also' creeps in, you are saying two things.
02The opposite test — Nobody ever says the opposite of 'We care about our customers.' A sentence with no possible opposite is not a message.
03The subject swap — If the line still works with a competitor's name in place of the brand's, it belongs to no one.
TIP
In a 15-second ad, the turn usually comes at 8–10 seconds. It takes nerve not to fill the last second with explanation.
What moves us
Being moved doesn't come from explaining emotion; it comes when the audience notices on their own. Instead of naming grief, you show the empty chair left at the table.
<small>Specifics</small>Numbers, things, time
Not 'many people' but 'a 3-shift worker at six a.m., just off duty'
<small>Turn</small>Where expectation breaks once
The story's 'turn'
In a 15-second ad, at 8–10 seconds
<small>Space</small>Room left for the audience to fill
Leave the conclusion unsaid

01Gather facts20 verified facts only, no adjectives
02Pick one personOne sentence on what is bothering one specific person right now
03Choose what to sayOf the 20, the one that matters only to that person
0430 sentencesSay it 30 ways. The first five usually get tossed
05Read aloudA line that doesn't roll off the tongue won't be remembered

The at-a-glance proposal

The power of planning comes from a document that gets read. Most student proposals are either pretty but unclear about what they propose, or full of content but unreadable. Reviewers and clients don't spend 3 minutes on one.
P12-PROCESS Knowing the processA wall covered in hand-drawn production-pipeline diagrams and sticky notes, a person tracing the flow with a finger
NoteKnowing the process — planning is not about ideas but about setting scope within the whole flow
One-line definition
This video makes [whom] feel [what] so that they [take what action]. If you can't fill in this sentence, it isn't a plan yet.
Planning starts by narrowing
The essence of planning is not generating ideas but setting scope. Write down the three constraints of budget, schedule and crew before you start, and the ideas actually get better.
A not-to-do list — Spell out the subjects you won't cover, the techniques you won't use and the information you won't include. Without it, revision requests multiply endlessly.
Success criteria — Write them as results, not completion. They must be checkable numbers: not 'views' but '40% watched to the end.'
TIP
State the conclusion on the first page and add evidence as you go. It is a proposal, not a report.

PART 12 wrap-up
One-page summary
11.1 How much production time has shrunk
Generation cost and time shrank; selection time didn't. Give figures with source and conditions.
11.2 How the pipeline was rebuilt
From linear to a generate↔select↔regenerate loop. Stop criteria · locked sections · version logs protect the schedule.
11.3 Where in the process it is actually used
Concentrated in variants · localization and VFX execution; shoot design, brand assets and strategy stay with people.
11.4 People: AI actors and digital doubles
Base image → reference input → character sheet → post-production fixes. Check likeness · scope · disclosure · records first.
11.5 Backgrounds: sets, LED walls, generated backgrounds
Choose among location · set · LED wall · chroma key+generation, but settle the background first, then light.
11.6 Elements and particles
Simulate the product and key physics; generate atmosphere and particles. Split into layers and composite.
11.7 Traditional production and AI production
Not rivals but tools for different jobs. Control the layers that carry brand assets; hand off the rest.
11.8 The Korean job market
What disappears is not jobs but the bottom rungs of the ladder. AI has become a requirement within existing roles.
11.9 Portfolio platforms
Label by process to the strictest rules and keep it the same on every channel. Inflating results is fatal.
11.10 Overseas markets and LinkedIn
What postings increasingly demand is not prompting but visual grammar · consistency · leadership. More demand doesn't mean higher rates.
11.11 Vision and expertise
Problem definition · reasoning · feel for the real · language skills keep their value. Be broom-shaped, but keep the vertical stroke.
11.12 Key message and copy
A message is a choice, not a summary. It passes the opposite test and the subject swap, and moves people through specifics · turn · space.
11.13 Planning and the proposal
One-line definition, not-to-do list, success criteria. In the 7-page structure, every page title must be a conclusion sentence.
11.14 Turning work into a job
Build with the folder rule and last-day 30 minutes, pick 5 pieces per role, explain each as 'intent-constraint-choice-result.'

If a video is complete only when the audience moves, who made it? This PART asks again, from where we stand today, the question Nam June Paik opened. When the screen leaves the rectangle, the audience turns from watchers into participants, and the work must run itself in a gallery for a month, most of what a video maker has learned is still useful. Only the way you use it changes.

Background 23
The man who turned television around
P13-CRTTOWER The origin of video art — a television towerAn installation of dozens of stacked CRT televisions playing abstract video in a dark gallery
NoteAn homage to Paik-style television towers — a form that stacked the receive-only box and turned it into a medium for making. "The More, the Better" used 1,003 sets

In 1963, "Exposition of Music — Electronic Television" opened in a small gallery in Wuppertal, Germany. Thirteen televisions stood in the room. Some had distorted pictures; on others the image changed when visitors pressed a foot pedal or made a sound into a microphone. It was the first solo show of Nam June Paik, born in Seoul in 1932, and is now called the starting point of video art.

Television then was a device for receiving at home whatever the broadcaster sent. Paik set out to reverse that one-way flow. He let viewers intervene in the picture, and later built his own video synthesizer for shaping the video signal by hand. He turned a medium of receiving into a medium of making.

He joined Fluxus in 1962, part of a movement erasing the line between everyday life and art, and after meeting John Cage in 1958 he brought an Eastern sense of time into his work. In "TV Buddha" (1974), a Buddha statue sits before a television, gazing at its own image relayed by a camera. Meditation and closed circuit, the cyclical time of the East and the electronics of the West meet on one screen.

His vision reached beyond the work, too. In a 1974 proposal to the Rockefeller Foundation he first used the term 'electronic superhighway,' 20 years before the internet became widely known. On January 1, 1984, he aired "Good Morning Mr. Orwell," a live broadcast linking New York, Paris and Seoul by satellite. Where Orwell had pictured 1984 as the year of surveillance, Paik set out that same year to show the other side: technology could also connect people.

"The More, the Better," built at the MMCA Gwacheon for the 1988 Seoul Olympics, is a tower of 1,003 televisions stacked 18.5 meters high. It went dark in 2018 and came back on in 2022 after 4 years and 7 months of conservation work. The restoration exposed media art's hardest problem. If its parts are discontinued, what does the work survive as? The conservation issues discussed later start here.
Further reading — Nam June Paik Art Center, The Return of Nam June Paik · MMCA, My Nam June Paik: Memory, Conservation, Expansion (2023) · Lev Manovich, The Language of New Media
PART 13Media art and expanded cinema
What is media art?

Media art is less a genre than an attitude. It is the umbrella term for work that takes the new media of its time as material and explores how those media change people and the world. In the 1960s that was television, in the 1990s the internet, and now sensors, data and generative models.
P13-INTERACTIVE Interactive media artAn installation where wall-filling particles of light swirl after visitors' hand gestures, with visitor silhouettes
NoteInteractive media art — the viewer's actions change the state of the work. Today's materials are sensors and data
Why there are so many names
<small>Video art</small>Late 1960s
Emerged as portable video gear spread
Twisting TV's language, or showing viewers themselves on closed circuit
<small>Media art</small>A broader name
Came into use as materials widened beyond video to computers, networks and sensors
<small>New media art</small>From the 1990s
Work premised on digital and the internet
Weakness: the 'new' grows old with time
<small>Post-internet art</small>After the internet became like air
A contested term with no agreed academic definition
Note
You don't need to memorize the terms. But borrow one to describe your work without knowing what it means, and reviewers will spot it at once.

PART 13Media art and expanded cinema
How video and media art differ

What's different? If you've read this far, you already have most of the skills you need. Reading a frame, building light, joining cuts and handling sound all still apply. What changes is not the skills but the premises.

Two things are the same. Both are time-based media, so length · rhythm · repetition · stillness are means of expression, and the production process of shooting · lighting · editing · grading · sound is still needed. The bigger the screen, the more your fundamentals show.
Regular video
Viewer position — seated in front of the screen
Start and end — fixed
Aspect ratio — can change to suit the medium
Equipment — a means of showing the result
Completion — done on delivery
Repetition — assumes a single viewing
Media art
Viewer position — enters and moves through the space
Start and end — viewers come and go at any time
Aspect ratio — a condition of the work; changing it is damage
Equipment — often part of the work
Completion — done only after running the whole show
Repetition — assumes hundreds of loops a day
TIP
Carry over a four-part arc as is, and most viewers see only the 'turn' and leave. It must read within 30 seconds from wherever they start watching.
What students miss most often: the start and end
<small>Loop design</small>Make the end join the start
If the last frame resembles the first, the seam disappears
<small>Entry points</small>Readable wherever they come in
Repeat the key image periodically
<small>Length</small>Between 2 and 7 minutes
Any longer and far fewer people watch to the end
Why you must keep the aspect ratio

Installation guidelines from media art conservation bodies specify that a work's aspect ratio be preserved, and state that enlarging or cropping to fit a screen is not proper practice. In video production, recutting for vertical is routine; with an artwork, that act itself changes the work. Here you must let go of the habit of reframing every time you change media.
Make exhibition video on the premise that nobody watches from the start. Making it readable from any entry point is the design.<small>13.2 How video and media art differ</small>

Re-edit one of your existing videos into an exhibition loop. Keep it under 3 minutes and structure it so the theme reads within 30 seconds from any starting point.
Tip
Show a friend 30 seconds from a random point and ask what the work is about. If two out of three get it, you pass.
Assessment
Is the seam invisible? Are the entry points designed?
Model answer
An edit that matched start and end on the same image and repeated the key motif every 40 seconds so it read from anywhere.

PART 13Media art and expanded cinema
Tool map
What do you make it with? An editing tool produces one fixed output, but media art tools usually make 'a program that keeps running in real time.' You design for operation, not completion.
P13-SENSOR Sensors and codeAn artist wiring a depth sensor and microcontroller at a workbench, a laptop showing code
NoteSensors and code — media art tools make not a finished product but a program that keeps running
Structure

Read interactive media art in three boxes: sensor input (camera · depth · mic · touch) → processing (TouchDesigner · Unity · p5.js) → output (projection · LED · sound). The tool map below follows the same order.
<small>Tools that make real-time video</small>Processing

TouchDesigner — Wire nodes together to make real-time video. Links sensors · sound · video · projection output in one window; the most widely used tool for exhibitions, free under a non-commercial license
Unreal Engine · Unity — Game engines. 3D space, VR · AR, virtual production. Camera and lighting concepts carry straight over
Processing · p5.js — Drawing with code. Generative basics; p5.js runs right in the browser, the lowest barrier to entry
Max/MSP · Pure Data — Sound and signal. For sound-led or sound-reactive work
<small>Tools that take input</small>Input
Depth camera — A person's distance and pose. The basic input for motion-reactive work
LiDAR — Scans space as points. Position tracking in large spaces, turning space into data
Arduino · Raspberry Pi — Small computers that run sensors and motors. Read light · sound · distance · pressure and turn it into video
Webcam and video analysis — One camera for motion detection, contour extraction, face tracking. The most realistic option with no budget
<small>Tools that send output</small>Output
Resolume — Plays and mixes video live. The standard for concert and club visuals
MadMapper — Dedicated to projection mapping. Fits video onto surfaces that aren't flat
NDI · Syphon — Channels for passing video between programs in real time. Essential once you have several machines

Don't pick the tool first. Write in one sentence 'what happens when the viewer does what,' then choose, and your options shrink to two or three.

PART 13Media art and expanded cinema
Making it work in the gallery
Working in the studio and working every day for a month in a gallery are entirely different problems. A media artwork's reputation usually turns not on polish but on 'was it ever off?'
P13-LEDROOM LED mirror roomAn infinity-mirror LED room reflecting visitors endlessly among points of light
NoteLED mirror room — it repeats hundreds of times a day and must stay on all month. Operation is part of the work
Light and distance
1/4Brightness when screen area quadruples. Brightness is rated in ANSI lumens; the same output looks dimmer on a bigger screen
About 3mDistance needed for a 2-meter-wide image with a 1.5 throw-ratio lens. Measure the space first, then choose the lens
Ambient light — In a brightly lit gallery, black lifts to gray. If dark areas matter, make light control a condition of the show.
Surface — A white wall is safest, but texture costs resolution. A dark surface deepens blacks but darkens everything.
Note
Screen savers, sleep mode and automatic updates are the most common causes of reboots during a show. Turn them all off.
Keeping it running
01Auto-start — When the power comes on, the program should launch itself with nobody there. OS auto-login and startup registration are the basics.
02No power saving — Turn off screen savers, sleep mode and automatic updates.
03Scheduled restart — Have it restart once every day before opening, and errors won't pile up.
04Backup version — Also export the work as a plain video file. If the real-time piece stops, you can at least play that.
What to bring on site
Item
Why

There are never enough outlets

Needed for both safety and looks

Lets you reproduce it exactly at the next show

On-site labels are often late
Safety and liability
01Cables — Keep cables out of visitor paths. If unavoidable, use covers.
02Brightness and flashing — Rapid flashing can trigger seizures in some viewers. Avoid more than three flashes in 1 second, and if there are any, post a notice at the entrance.
03Sound — Set volume and direction so you don't affect neighboring works. Consider directional speakers or headphones.
04Cameras and privacy — If the work captures viewers on camera, state whether it records; if it doesn't store footage, say so.
Design for the last day of the show, not the first. Still running a month later is part of the work.<small>13.5 Making it work in the gallery</small>

PART 13Media art and expanded cinema
Artwork statements and portfolios

In media art, writing is part of the work. Viewers read the statement to understand the piece, and open calls and residencies are judged on text and photos alone. The demands differ from a video portfolio, so practice separately.
Anatomy of a statement
01What it isStart with 'This work is …' Open with background and nobody reads to the end
02HowWhat happens when the viewer does what. The user manual for an interactive work
03WhyThe reason it must take this form. Grounds for a choice, not a tech showcase
TIP
Gallery wall texts of 150 to 300 characters get read. Any longer and nobody stands there reading.
Words to avoid
Vague big words — 'existence', 'relationship', 'boundary' used without explanation say nothing at all. If you use one, state concretely, at least once, what it refers to in this work.
Listing tech — tools belong in the materials line. Showing off tools in the statement makes the work look small.
Unverified quotations — don't quote books you haven't read. It's the first thing jurors ask about.

Documentation keeps the work alive

A media art work vanishes when the show closes. Only the documentation remains, and the next open call and the next exhibition are decided by it. During the show, be sure to shoot installation views, details, real audience reactions, and even the installation process.
The most important day in the gallery is not opening day but the day you shoot documentation.<small>13.6 Artwork statements and portfolios</small>

PART 13Media art and expanded cinema
Three debates
Immersion, AI, preservation. Study media art and you will run into three debates. None has a settled answer, so the goal is to know the grounds of each position and decide where you stand.
Debate one — immersive exhibitions: art or product
The product view
One Korean study defines immersive exhibitions as 'commercial content aimed at the immersive experience itself, beyond mediating art'
Admission — immersive shows abroad charge adults tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand won; Korean public museums mostly around KRW 10,000
An industry CEO admits — 'anyone can take on a theme like waves, so borrowed ideas and copyright infringement are hard to prove'
The necessity view
When everything can be watched at home, immersive experience gives people a reason to show up in person
Public museums are absorbing it too — MMCA's 2026 exhibition on light, the Seoul Museum of Art's new-media branch
A question to consider

Is a work made on a KRW 1.5 million budget and shown four hours each evening on a city screen the same media art as a ticketed venue drawing millions a year? What divides them: the medium, the source of money, or where the audience stands?
Term
Two strands of authorship — work that uses AI as a tool differs from work that takes AI itself as its subject. It is the difference between using a tool and questioning it.
Debate two — generative AI and authorship
<small>The 2024 gap</small>There were no rules
A generative AI entry won the grand prize in a public-service ad contest, then sparked controversy
The organizer said 'with no AI clause, we can neither block nor encourage it', and the award stood
<small>The 2026 shift</small>Disclosure, not bans
JoongAng Media Art Competition — AI assistance encouraged, heavy use judged in a separate category, use and scope must be disclosed
Veterans Affairs ministry call — asks for tools used · scope · even reference sources
An international conference's art track — stating AI's role is mandatory
<small>Work that questions the tool</small>2026 Korea Artist Prize finalist
Restores a 1946 film with AI, revealing that 'technology cannot fully restore history'
Examines the biases built into video-generation models
In 2 years, 'AI use: no rules' became 'AI use: must be declared.' The habit of logging in your production journal which tools you used, where, and how much becomes your submission paperwork.
Debate three — how a work survives
737unitsDamaged CRTs in the restoration of The More, the Better, repaired or replaced with used parts
266unitsSmall monitors at the top, replaced with flat displays that keep the original look. Eight videos converted to digital
4 days a week, 2hoursOperating time since the September 2022 restart, to protect the work

The open question — is The More, the Better, with its CRTs swapped for flat screens, still the same work? Conservation guidelines divide installations into cases where 'the equipment is part of the work itself' and where it is 'used only to show the work.' In the first case, replacing equipment means changing the work.
What students can do now — document the software and versions, hardware, settings, and 'what may change and what must not,' and the work can be restaged years later.
Preservation as a career — in 2026 MMCA opened a training program for conservators, new media included. Not only making work but keeping it is becoming a profession.
On the day you finish a work, write a one-page tech spec. That sheet becomes the key to switching the work back on 10 years later.<small>13.8 Three debates</small>
<small>Exercise</small>13.8
Task
Choose one of the three debates and write a 1,000-character opinion piece. Present the grounds of each side, then state your position and give your reasons.
Tip
Find and write down the arguments against your position first. If you don't know the counterarguments, your own position is weak too.
Assessment
Are both sides' grounds presented fairly? Does the conclusion come with reasons?
Model answer
An essay that draws on the writer's own work to turn an abstract debate into a concrete case.
PART 13 wrap-up
One-page summary
13.1 What media art is
An attitude, not a genre. Just check that you can say in one sentence why it has to be this medium.
13.2 How video and media art differ
The premises differ, not the technology. Viewers walk in midway, so design the loop and entry points, and respect the aspect ratio.
13.3 The Korean media art landscape
Three strands: institutions · city screens · the immersive industry. Students get onto city screens first and build a track record.
13.4 A map of tools
Split it into processing · input · output. Write what happens when the viewer does what, then choose tools.
13.5 Making it run in the gallery
Calculate throw ratio and brightness, and keep it running to the last day with auto-start · sleep disabled · daily restart · a backup copy.
13.6 Statements and portfolios
What · how · why, in 150–300 characters. Don't leave out the materials line · system diagram · installation requirements · contribution, and shoot documentation.
13.7 Open calls and grants
Start with calls that have a student category. In one semester, prepare all four: Korean artist statement · English proposal · 30-second highlight · 3-minute film.
13.8 Three debates
The nature of immersive shows, disclosure standards for AI, discontinued parts and preservation. Know each side's grounds and decide where you stand.

prologue.html: Prologue · BEFORE YOU SHOOT
The basic units of the screen

First, get hold of the ten words you need to read this book: frame, aspect ratio, resolution, frame rate, shutter, cut, scene, sequence, take and platform specs. It is a short, four-page dictionary, but every sentence in the PARTs that follow is built on these words.
PrologueThe basic units of the screen
Frame and aspect ratio
The frame is the border formed by the screen's four edges; the aspect ratio is the relationship between its width and height. These two decide, before anything else, what goes in and what gets cut.
P00-FRAME Camera monitor showing frame guidesWhite guide lines and a safe-area box over a street scene
Note The guides on a camera monitor preview what stays and what gets cut in the final ratio
Aspect ratio is written as width divided by height. 16:9 is 1.78; CinemaScope is 2.39. Vertical video flips the same numbers and is called 9:16.
Ratio
Typical resolution
Used for
Old TVs and monitors, archive footage, deliberate retro looks
Standard horizontal spec for broadcast · YouTube · lecture video
Flat format for theatrical screening; feels almost the same as 16:9
CinemaScope, wide monitors, letterboxed ads
Instagram feed, carousels, profile videos
Vertical Instagram feed post; the feed format that fills the most screen
Shorts · Reels · TikTok · Stories, full vertical screen
Vertical LED signage, full screen on some smartphones
Equirectangular projection for 360-degree VR video, twice as wide as tall
16:9The horizontal standard, TV and YouTube
9:16Full vertical screen, short-form and stories
21:9The cinematic feel of theaters and ads
1:1A square in the feed, carousels
P00-RATIOS One scene, three ratiosA 16:9 TV, a letterboxed wide monitor, a phone held upright
Note Change the ratio and even the same scene shows a different area and a different subject size
Term

Safe area — the inner zone for key information, in case the screen edges are cropped or covered by UI. Broadcast kept the outer 10% clear; today the spots covered by platform buttons and captions play that role.

Decide the ratio before you start shooting: shoot horizontal and crop to vertical, and 2/3 of the frame is gone. If you must deliver in several ratios, keep the subject centered with room on both sides.
<small>Exercise</small>0.1
Task
Turn on your phone camera's grid and, from the same spot, take one photo each at 16:9, 1:1 and 9:16. Mark what got cut off.
Tip
Don't move the subject; only turn the camera. What the ratio changes is not the subject but how much of the surroundings you see.
PrologueThe basic units of the screen
Resolution · frame rate · shutter
How dense each picture is, how many are shown in 1 second, how long each was exposed. These are the three numbers that set the texture of video.
1080p1920×1080, FHD. The delivery default
4KUHD3840×2160, four times the area of FHD
24fpsThe convention for film and brand films
30fpsBroadcast · explainer video; 60fps for sports · slow motion
P00-FPS Frames per second — a sequence of stills becomes motionTwelve sequential photos of a water drop laid out like film on a lightbox
Note Video is, in the end, a series of stills; how many are shown in 1 second decides how smooth the motion is
Pixels add up to a picture
16 × 9 = 144 pixelsYou see dots
64 × 36 = 2,304 pixelsYou see shapes
256 × 144You see expressions
1920 × 1080 = 2.07 million pixelsFHD — the pixels disappear

Resolution = number of dotsFHD is 4 times HD, 4K is 4 times FHD, 8K is 4 times 4KAt the same screen size, more dots look sharper; with the same number of dots, a bigger screen looks coarser (LED pitch)Shoot in 4K and deliver in FHD, and you can crop in up to two times and stay sharp
Figure 0-1 Resolution and pixels — the same photo drawn with 144, 2,304, 36,000 and 2.07 million dots. The moment the dots disappear is "image quality."
<small>Resolution</small>Number of dots
Width×height in pixels. 1920×1080 is about 2.07 million
Higher stays crisp even when shown large, but files get bigger
Choose to suit screen size and viewing distance
<small>Frame rate</small>Frames per second
Written as fps. 24 for film, 30 for broadcast, 60 for sports and games
Shoot high and play back slow for slow motion
Keep one value throughout a project
<small>Shutter</small>Exposure time per frame
Slow shutter speed makes motion smear; fast makes it stutter
180-degree rule — shutter speed at twice the frame rate (for 24fps, 1/48 s)
The baseline for natural motion blur
TIP
Shoot in 4K and deliver in FHD, and the edit gains room to punch in or recrop for vertical. That reframing room can only be created at the shoot.

Set the three numbers once before the shoot and keep them to the end. Change them midway and frames double up or drop out in the edit, and image quality turns uneven. Delivery specs come first; work the camera settings backward from them.
<small>Exercise</small>0.2
Task
Shoot the same movement once at 24fps and once at 60fps, play them side by side, and write one sentence on which looks 'cinematic' and which looks 'lifelike.'
Tip
Set the shutter speed to 1/48 s and 1/120 s respectively, and you see the difference made by frame rate alone.
PrologueThe basic units of the screen
Cut · scene · sequence · take
These are the units for counting video. If the set and the edit suite don't use the same words, people picture different things for the same scene.
P00-TIMELINE Cut · scene · sequence are units of the timelineClips grouped into colored blocks and a hand on a shuttle wheel
Note On the edit timeline, one clip is a cut, a same-color group is a scene, and a group of groups is a sequence
01FrameA single still picture. A 15-second ad at 24fps is 360 frames
02Cut (shot)One unbroken run of the camera. A 15-second ad usually has 6–12 cuts
03SceneA group of cuts at the same place · same time. Counted as the kitchen scene, the street scene
04SequenceA group of scenes forming one event. A 15-second ad is usually a single problem–solution sequence
Cut — the unit of editing
One continuous stretch of picture in the finished piece
What the editor cuts and joins
"Lots of cuts" means a fast editing rhythm
Take — the unit of shooting
One attempt at shooting a cut. Take 1, take 2
Every "one more" on set adds a take
Editing means choosing one of several takes

Coverage means shooting a scene broken into several sizes and angles. Only with a wide cut showing everything, a medium cut on the people and close-ups of faces and hands does the edit suite have choices. A scene shot without coverage can't be edited; it has to be reshot.
<small>Exercise</small>0.3
Task
Pick a 15-second ad you like, count its cuts, and make a table of how many scenes it divides into.
Tip
Pause every time the picture changes. Consecutive cuts in the same place belong to one scene.

Horizontal, vertical and platform specs
The same video gets a different ratio, length and covered area depending on where it is posted. The platform is not the last variable in planning; it is the first condition.

Note A vertical frame shows faces and hands large but gives up the context on either side

Note
Platforms change length limits and UI layout often. Recheck the platform's current specs right before delivery.

Horizontal video often moves from the situation in to the person; vertical often starts with the person and adds the situation after. To make both formats from the same material, don't just crop; restructure.
Reading order for this book

This book puts practice ahead of theory. First you learn to read the screen in the language of video, decide what to shoot through planning (storyboard · PPM), then finish a piece through shooting, lighting · sound and editing, in that order. Next come media specs, ad cases, platforms, industry · careers and the AI shift, and finally a return to history, theory and media art. History and theory read after you have made something with your own hands become things you can explain, not things to memorize.

Task

Take a screenshot of a video on the platform you watch most, shade in the areas covered by buttons · captions · account name with a pen, and estimate and note what share of the screen is left as safe area.
Tip
